food.text: The world's earliest eating establishments recognizable as restaurants in the modern sense first emerged in Song dynasty China during the 11th and 12th centuries. Street food had already become an integral part of Chinese food culture in the 7th century, during the Tang dynasty.
During the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368), contacts with the West brought a major food crop, sorghum, to China. Other foreign food products and methods of preparation arrived along with it.
In the Song dynasty (960–1279), rice had become the major staple crop of the poor. A normal Chinese meal was built on grains, vegetables and fish, with very little red meat.
Hu Sihui, a Mongol doctor of Chinese medicine, compiled the Yinshan Zhengyao, a guide to cooking and health. It brought together Chinese and Mongol food practices under the Yuan dynasty.

Yunnan cuisine is unique in China for cheeses like Rubing and Rushan, made by the Bai people, and for its yogurt. The yogurt may owe something to Mongolian influence during the Yuan dynasty, Central Asian settlement in Yunnan, and the proximity and influence of India and Tibet.
The Yinshan Zhengyao features recipes with Central Asian influence, mostly in northern China. Its dishes reflect the exchanges that shaped the food of the Mongol court.

Hu Sihui presented the Yinshan Zhengyao to Tugh Temür in 1330, at the height of Mongol power. Food scholars see it as evidence of Middle Eastern influence on Mongol food culture, comparable to the Columbian exchange.
The Yinshan Zhengyao is known from a 1456 Ming Dynasty edition manuscript. It also survives in fragments from the Yuan dynasty.

In the Yinshan Zhengyao, the medicinal recipes give step-by-step instructions for each ingredient, followed by the cooking methods for those ingredients. The layout lets readers avoid lingering over descriptions of the cooking.

art.text: The Yuan dynasty's painting is characterized by the work of the so-called Four Great Masters. The most notable was Huang Gongwang (1269–1354), whose cool and restrained landscapes were admired by his contemporaries and by Chinese literati painters of later centuries.

The height of the classical Chinese architectural tradition in writing and illustration is found in the Yingzao Fashi, a building manual. It was written by 1100 and published in 1103 by Li Jie (1065–1110).
Historians note that Chinese painting had a profound influence on Tibetan painting in general. Starting from the 14th and 15th century, Tibetan painting incorporated many elements from Chinese art.

Ni Zan (1301–1374), another of the Yuan dynasty's Four Great Masters, often arranged his compositions with a strong, distinct foreground and background. He left the middle-ground as an empty expanse. Later Ming and Qing dynasty painters frequently adopted this scheme.
China is the birthplace of the kite, and Weifang is one of the chief places where Chinese kites originated. Kite-flying became prevalent in Weifang during the Song dynasty (960–1279).

Li Jie's Yingzao Fashi, published in 1103, contains numerous meticulous illustrations and diagrams. They show how halls and building components were assembled, and the book also classifies structure types and building components.
Chinese knotting is a decorative handicraft that began as a form of folk art in the Tang and Song dynasty (AD 960–1279). It creates decorative knot patterns, and it was later popularized in the Ming.

Ivory was not a prestigious material in the rather strict hierarchy of Chinese art, where jade had always been far more highly regarded. Ivory and bone had been used since early times, when China still had its own species of elephant, but demand for ivory seems to have played a large part in their extinction, which came before 100 BC. During the Ming dynasty, ivory began to be used for small statuettes of gods and others.
art.source_title: Chinese art by medium and technique

art.text: By the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), kite-flying in Weifang had become even more popular, and kite fairs on a rather large scale had appeared. Kites were sold across Shandong and also to Jiangsu, Fujian, Anhui and other places.

war.text: In 1115 the Jurchen tribes revolted against their Liao overlords and founded the Jin dynasty. In 1125 the devastating Jin cataphract annihilated the Liao dynasty. Jin's invasion of the Song dynasty followed swiftly.

In 1127 Kaifeng was sacked in a massive catastrophe known as the Jingkang Incident, which ended the Northern Song dynasty. Later the entire north of China was conquered by the Jin. The surviving members of the Song court regrouped in the new capital of Hangzhou. There they began the Southern Song dynasty, which ruled territories south of the Huai River.

The Mongol conquest ended the era of divided rule in China piece by piece. Western Xia fell in 1227, the Jin dynasty in 1234, and finally the Southern Song dynasty in 1279 after a protracted and bloody war. The Song capital Hangzhou fell in 1276, and the Song navy was annihilated at the Battle of Yamen in 1279. During the conquest the population sharply dwindled, and the census fell from about 120 million before the invasion to roughly 60 million in 1300, though historians dispute how much of that was killing rather than missed records, enserfment or plague.
The earliest use of Chinese prototype firearms occurred at an 1132 siege during the Jin-Song Wars. Firearms thus first appeared on the battlefield in the conflict between the Jin and the Song.
war.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

war.text: The Song fought a significant war against the Vietnamese kingdom of Đại Việt from 1075 to 1077 over a border dispute and the Song's severing of commercial relations with Đại Việt. Vietnamese forces first inflicted heavy damage in a raid on Guangxi, after which Song commander Guo Kui penetrated as far as Thăng Long, modern Hanoi. Both sides suffered heavy losses, which prompted the Vietnamese commander Thường Kiệt to make peace overtures. Captured territories and prisoners of war were mutually exchanged in 1082.
When the Jin dynasty destroyed the Liao, remnants of the Liao court fled to Central Asia. There they founded the Qara Khitai Empire, also called the Western Liao dynasty.

In the 13th century the Mongol Empire conquered China and established the Yuan dynasty, which lasted from 1271 to 1368. The Southern Song fell in 1279 after a protracted and bloody war. In the 14th century epidemics of plague killed an estimated quarter of the population of China, and natural disasters and corrupt governance set off widespread peasant uprisings from the 1340s. Han rule returned in 1368, when Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty and proclaimed himself the Hongwu Emperor.
The oldest surviving bronze hand cannon dates to 1288, during the Yuan period. It is a rare physical survivor from the early years of gunpowder weapons in China.
war.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

war.text: After the Mongol invasions of Japan (1274–1281), a Japanese scroll painting depicted explosive bombs used by Yuan-dynasty forces against their samurai. The picture is a rare artistic record of gunpowder weapons in action.
war.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

literature.text: The Song (960–1279) and Yuan (1271–1368) dynasties were notable for their lyrics (ci), essays, dramas, and plays. Earlier dynasties such as the Han and Tang were considered the golden ages of poetry.

Bi Sheng (990–1051) invented movable type printing during the Song dynasty. Together with the widespread woodblock printing introduced in the Tang, it rapidly spread written knowledge throughout China.
Several of the Song dynasty's greatest poets were also capable government officials. They included Ouyang Xiu (1007–1072), Su Shi (1037–1101), and Wang Anshi (1021–1086).

The ci form flourished under the Song as a few hundred songs became standard templates for poems. Each template had its own distinctive and variously set meter, so poets wrote new words to established patterns.
Additional musical influences contributed to the Yuan dynasty's distinctive qu opera culture. They also spawned the sanqu form, a type of individual poem based on it.

The free and expressive style of Song high culture has been contrasted with the majestic poems of the Tang. Ever since the Song itself, poets and critics have debated the merits of Song poetry relative to the earlier work.
Sima Guang's compilation of the Zizhi Tongjian was presented to Emperor Shenzong of Song in 1084. It is a landmark of the Chinese tradition of history writing during the Song dynasty.
Elaborate allegorical readings of the Classic of Poetry went unquestioned until the 12th century. Then the scholar Zheng Qiao (1104–1162) first wrote down his scepticism of them.

The Tibetan scholar Sakya Pandita (1182–1251) was a well-known scholar of Sanskrit. He promoted the study of Sanskrit secular disciplines among Tibetans, showing how Indian learning shaped the literature of Himalayan cultures.
The Franciscan friar Odoric of Pordenone traveled in the East from 1304 to 1330, and visited friars in Hangzhou and Zhangzhou. China's Franciscans were mentioned in his writings, the Itinerarium.
literature.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

science.text: Su Song began an astronomical clock tower in Kaifeng in 1086 and finished it in 1092. It was driven by an escapement mechanism and featured the earliest known chain drive. The tower held an armillary sphere, a celestial globe and a mechanical chronograph.

The Chinese description of a gunpowder formula dates to 1044, during the Song dynasty. Roger Bacon recorded the earliest known European recipe in his Opus Majus of 1267, more than two centuries later.
science.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

science.text: The compass, gunpowder, papermaking and printing are known as the Four Great Inventions. They were among China's most important technological advances, and Europe only learned of them by the end of the Middle Ages.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in China

science.text: China was a global scientific and technological leader until the early years of the Ming dynasty. Chinese scientific activity began to wane around the fourteenth century. One suggested factor is the imperial examination system, which gave scholars little incentive to pursue science.

In 1127, the invading Jurchen army dismantled Su Song's clock tower upon taking the capital of Kaifeng. The armillary sphere was brought to Beijing, but the tower was never successfully reinstated, not even by Su Song's son. Two versions of his treatise survive, so the tower can still be studied.

In 1070, Su Song compiled the Ben Cao Tu Jing, or Illustrated Pharmacopoeia, with a team of scholars. Its source material dated from 1058 to 1061. The treatise also covered botany, zoology, mineralogy and metallurgy.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in China

science.text: Shen Kuo took an interdisciplinary approach to archaeology. He incorporated his findings into studies on metallurgy, optics, astronomy, geometry and ancient music measures. He criticized the belief that ancient vessels were products of 'sages' and not common people.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in China

science.text: The earliest use of Chinese prototype firearms occurred at an 1132 siege during the Jin-Song Wars. The oldest surviving bronze hand cannon dates to 1288, during the Yuan period.
science.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

science.text: The first known Chinese description of the formula for gunpowder dates to 1044, during the Song dynasty. The earliest known European recipe came more than two centuries later, in Roger Bacon's Opus Majus of 1267.
science.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

science.text: Su Song's celestial atlas of 1092 is one of the oldest existent star maps in printed form. It was included in the horological treatise on his clock tower.

Ouyang Xiu (1007 to 1072) compiled an analytical catalogue of ancient rubbings on stone and bronze. Patricia B. Ebrey says it pioneered ideas in early epigraphy and archaeology. Later, Hong Mai (1123 to 1202) used ancient Han dynasty vessels to debunk false descriptions in the Bogutu catalogue.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in China

politics.text: Kublai Khan officially proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in the traditional Han style in 1271, though the conquest was not complete until 1279, when the Southern Song was defeated in the Battle of Yamen. It was the first dynasty founded by a non-Han ethnicity that ruled all of China proper.

The Ming dynasty was founded by Zhu Yuanzhang in 1368, following the collapse of the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. In 1367 the dynastic head of the Red Turbans suspiciously died while a guest of Zhu, leaving no one able to contest his march to the throne. Zhu's army then advanced on the Yuan capital Dadu, and he declared the founding of the Ming dynasty only after razing the Yuan palaces there to the ground. He took the era name Hongwu, "Vastly Martial", and later made Nanjing the capital. The Ming was the last imperial dynasty of China ruled by the Han people.

In July 1449 the Oirat leader Esen Tayisi invaded Ming China. Encouraged by the chief eunuch Wang Zhen, the Zhengtong Emperor led a force personally, and on 8 September Esen routed his army and captured him. This event is known as the Tumu Crisis.

The Hongwu Emperor enfeoffed his many sons throughout China and tried to guide them with the Huang-Ming Zuxun, a set of published dynastic instructions. This failed when his teenage successor, the Jianwen Emperor, tried to curtail his uncle's power and arrested many of the Prince of Yan's associates. The Prince of Yan answered with the Jingnan campaign, a rebellion that became a three-year civil war. In it the palace in Nanjing was burned to the ground, and the Jianwen Emperor, his wife, his mother and his courtiers burned with it. The Prince of Yan took the throne as the Yongle Emperor in 1402.

In 1403 the Yongle Emperor announced that the new capital of China would be Beijing, his power base, demoting Nanjing to a secondary capital. Construction of the new city lasted from 1407 to 1420 and employed hundreds of thousands of workers daily. At its center stood the Forbidden City, the palatial residence of the emperor and his family.

After the Zhengtong Emperor's capture, his younger brother took the throne as the Jingtai Emperor, which made the captive a useless bargaining chip. Defense minister Yu Qian gained control of the Ming armed forces and repelled the Oirats, who then released the former emperor. He was kept under house arrest until the 1457 coup called the Wresting the Gate Incident, after which he retook the throne as the Tianshun Emperor.

Cai Jing, appointed by Emperor Zhezong, remained in power until 1125. He revived the New Policies and pursued political opponents, tolerated corruption, and encouraged Emperor Huizong to neglect his duties to focus on artistic pursuits. A peasant rebellion led by Fang La broke out in Zhejiang and Fujian in 1120.

In 1336 Toghon Temür, the last Mongol ruler of the Yuan dynasty in China before the retreat to Mongolia, sent an embassy including Genoese Italians to Pope Benedict XII requesting a new archbishop. The pope answered in 1342 by sending legates and ecclesiastical leaders to Khanbaliq, including Giovanni de Marignolli.
politics.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

politics.text: The Yuan dynasty passed laws against Muslims and Semu. In 1329 foreign holy men, including Muslims, lost their tax exemptions, and in 1328 the position of Muslim Qadi was abolished. From 1357 to 1367 a Persian garrison in Quanzhou revolted against the Yuan; the Persian official Yawuna assassinated the revolt's two leaders, Amin ud-Din and Saif ud-Din, in 1362 and took control of the rebels, until loyalist forces from Fuzhou defeated them in 1367.

philosophy.text: Chinese philosophy absorbed influences from Indian Buddhism over the centuries. This blending gave rise to Neo-Confucianism in the Song and Ming dynasties.
Beginning in the Song dynasty, the Confucian classics were the basis of the imperial exams. They became the core philosophy of the scholar-official class.

Buddhist scholars living under the Liao dynasty predicted that the mofa, an age in which the three treasures of Buddhism would be destroyed, would begin in the year 1052. Earlier dynasties, including the Sui and Tang, had also worried about the mofa, but they predicted different start dates.

A resurgent Neo-Confucianism, led by thinkers such as Zhu Xi (1130 to 1200), became the dominant school of thought in later Chinese dynasties such as the Song and Ming. The imperial state promoted it.

Wang Yangming (1472 to 1529) led a resurgent Neo-Confucianism during the Ming dynasty, which lasted from 1368 to 1644. The same school also became dominant in Korea's Joseon dynasty, which began in 1392.

Other schools rose to prominence in Chinese history besides Confucianism. The Lingbao school flourished during the Song dynasty, while the Quanzhen School developed in the 13th and 14th centuries under the Yuan dynasty. Later Taoist traditions were also influenced by Chinese Buddhism.

As early as the Sui dynasty, efforts were made to preserve Buddhist teachings by carving them into stone or burying them. These efforts continued under the Liao, with Emperor Xingzong funding several projects in the years immediately before 1052.
The Liao began printing Buddhist texts in the 990s, and an entire copy of the Tripitaka was completed in 1075. Portions of it have been found in a pagoda built in 1056.

Manichaeism later blended with Buddhism, Taoism and folk beliefs in China. The Xiapu Manuscript of Fujian Province, discovered in 2008, was probably written during the Ming dynasty. Special masters in Xiapu County still keep Ming-style books on mantras and rituals.

culture.text: Thousands of Europeans are thought to have lived in Yuan-dynasty China, arriving mostly in the second half of the 13th century and the first half of the 14th century. They came as visitors, traders and Christian missionaries, in years when the Mongol Empire connected Europe with the Yuan capital, Khanbaliq, modern Beijing.
culture.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

culture.text: Chinese culture was commercialized in the Song dynasty (960 to 1279), and the distinctions between social groups became blurred. Education centered on imperial examinations, which required essays and mastery of the Confucian classics. Those who passed the highest level became elite scholar-officials known as jinshi, a highly esteemed position.

The Yongle Emperor and his successors strongly patronised Tibetan Buddhism through construction, printing of sutras and ceremonies. Yongle tried to portray himself as a Buddhist ideal king, a cakravartin, and evidence suggests this persuaded foreign audiences.

The Franciscan friar Odoric of Pordenone made travels from 1304 to 1330 and visited friars in Hangzhou and Zhangzhou. He wrote about China's Franciscans in his Itinerarium, though he first returned to Europe in 1330.
culture.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages

culture.text: Evidence of a Tamil Hindu community in medieval China comes from Quanzhou in Fujian province. It includes a Tamil-Chinese bilingual inscription dated April 1281, devoted to the deity Śiva. Over 300 artifacts, idols and Chola-style temple structures have been discovered in Fujian province since 1933.

The Khitans, who ruled the Liao, considered the Buddha a protective deity and named him "The Benevolent King Who Guards the Country." They invoked Buddhism whenever they went to war and made massive offerings to placate the souls of fallen soldiers.

Buddhist scholars under the Liao dynasty predicted that the mofa, an age in which the three treasures of Buddhism would be destroyed, would begin in 1052. Emperor Xingzong funded several projects in the years just before 1052. Such efforts to preserve teachings by carving them into stone or burying them dated back to the Sui dynasty.

Hindu communities, particularly through Tamil merchant guilds of Ayyavole and Manigramam, once thrived in medieval south China. Evidence of Tamil Shiva motifs and temples, such as in the Kaiyuan temple, continues to be discovered in Quanzhou, Fujian.

Zoroastrians in China called their places of worship fire temples. Its followers did not preach in China or translate scriptures, so only the Hu people, not the Han Chinese, practiced it. Zoroastrianism eventually disappeared in China after the fall of the Song dynasty in 1279.

In 1333 Nicolaus de Bentra, chosen by Pope John XXII, officially replaced John de Montecorvino, and by 1338 there were complaints about the archbishop's absence. Toghon Temür, the last Mongol ruler of the Yuan dynasty in China, had sent an embassy including Genoese Italians to Pope Benedict XII in 1336, requesting a new archbishop. The pope sent legates in 1342, including Giovanni de Marignolli.
culture.source_title: Europeans in China during the Middle Ages
